text:
**Recommendation:** use a token bucket per customer, with the bucket size set to the full per-minute quota and the refill rate set to quota/60 per second. Enforce it in each region against a local, in-memory (or regional Redis) counter, and share quota across regions by *pre-allocating slices* of each customer's bucket to regions and rebalancing asynchronously. Make the limiter fail open on a hard deadline of about 2 ms. Return standard headers and a Retry-After on every 429. This keeps the hot path local (no cross-region round trip), tolerates bursts by design, and bounds the damage when it is wrong.

**Algorithm and why it suits bursty clients.** A token bucket lets a client spend up to its capacity instantly and then refills continuously. A paying client with 600/min has a 600-token bucket refilling at 10/s, so a job that sends 600 requests in two seconds succeeds fully and then simply waits for refill. A fixed-window counter would also allow that burst, but it permits double-spend at window boundaries (a client can send 600 at 12:00:59 and 600 at 12:01:00, so up to 2x quota in two seconds) and gives a cliff-edge reset that synchronizes retry storms. A sliding-window log is accurate but stores one entry per request (up to 6,000 per customer), which is too heavy for a 5 ms budget. A sliding-window counter approximation smooths boundaries but would reject the legitimate two-second burst whenever the previous window was busy. Leaky bucket as a queue would delay or shape the burst, which punishes exactly the behavior we want to allow. The token bucket's state is two numbers (tokens, last-refill timestamp), so a check is one tiny atomic update.

**Where state lives and how three regions share one quota.** Each region keeps a bucket per customer in a regional store (Redis in-region, with a small in-process cache in front of it). A single global store would put a cross-region round trip (tens to well over 100 ms) on every request, which blows the 5 ms budget outright, so it is rejected. Instead, the customer's quota is divided into per-region *allocations*. Start by splitting evenly (200/200/200 of a 600 quota) or by recent traffic share. Each region admits requests against its local allocation with zero cross-region latency. A background process every 1 to 2 seconds exchanges usage between regions (gossip or a small global coordinator that is off the request path) and shifts allocation toward regions with demand: a region that is exhausted borrows unused tokens from the others. Because a client's requests can land anywhere and often cluster by network location, rebalancing matters; without it a client whose traffic all lands in one region would be limited to a third of its quota.

**What the design gets wrong, and by how much.** There are three error sources. First, *under-enforcement from sync lag*: between rebalances, regions spend independently, so a customer can exceed quota. In the worst case, if every region's slice were generously over-provisioned, a customer could receive up to roughly 3x quota for the length of a sync interval. With the allocations summing to the quota, the overshoot is bounded much more tightly: it is roughly the tokens borrowed in flight, on the order of one sync interval of refill (about 1 to 2 seconds, so 10 to 20 requests at 600/min, 100 to 200 at 6,000/min), or 2 to 3% of a minute's quota in typical operation. Second, *over-enforcement (false 429s)*: a client bursting entirely into one region can be rejected while the other regions hold idle tokens, until the next rebalance moves them. For a 600/min customer with an even split, a two-second burst landing in one region could be throttled after about 200 requests even though 400 tokens sat elsewhere, for up to one sync interval. This is the more customer-visible error, and it is why borrowing should also be available synchronously and rarely: on local exhaustion, one best-effort, 2 ms-bounded request to a peer for a chunk of tokens, falling back to a 429 if it times out. Third, *free-tier slop*: at 60/min with three slices of 20, small integer slices make the error proportionally larger, so free accounts should use larger relative borrow chunks or a single home region. I accept all of this deliberately: the limiter exists to protect capacity and enforce fairness, not to bill, and a few percent of drift is cheaper than latency or an availability dependency. Any invoicing-grade metering must use a separate, exact pipeline.

**When the store is slow or down.** Every limiter call carries a hard timeout of about 2 ms (leaving headroom inside the 5 ms budget). On timeout or error, the limiter *fails open*: the request is admitted, and the failure is counted. Failing closed would let the limiter take the API down, which the requirement forbids. Add a circuit breaker so that after several consecutive failures the limiter skips the store entirely for a few seconds, avoiding the 2 ms tax on every request. During the outage, fall back to a coarse in-process per-instance limiter with a generous ceiling (for example, quota divided by expected instance count, times a safety factor) so that a single abusive client cannot saturate the service while the store is dark. This degrades accuracy, not availability. Clients see nothing unusual during fail-open: normal 200s, with rate-limit headers omitted or marked stale. Alert on fail-open rate, since a silent unlimited API is itself a risk.

**What clients see and how they learn limits.** Every response carries RateLimit-Limit (the plan quota), RateLimit-Remaining (the best estimate from the local region), and RateLimit-Reset (seconds until the bucket is full again), following the IETF draft header conventions. A rejection is HTTP 429 with a Retry-After header in seconds, computed as the time until at least one token (or a sensible minimum such as 1 second) is available, plus small server-side jitter so a fleet of rejected clients does not retry in lockstep. The body should be a short machine-readable error naming the limit and plan. Document the burst behavior explicitly: the full minute's quota may be spent at once and refills continuously at quota/60 per second. Because Remaining is regional and can lag, document it as approximate. Well-behaved clients should honor Retry-After and use exponential backoff with jitter on repeated 429s.

**Open questions and caveats.** Confirm with the business whether a few percent overshoot is acceptable for 6,000/min plans. Decide whether bursts should have an upper cap below the full quota for the largest tier, since 6,000 requests in two seconds is a 3,000 rps spike that the backend must absorb regardless of the limiter. Consider a separate, small per-second ceiling as a backend-protection guard. Finally, test the rebalancing under skewed traffic and region failure, since a lost region's allocation must be redistributed quickly.
